baby_tomb.title: The Small Human-Shaped Marker
baby_tomb.description: A small human-shaped marker, as thin as a page of stone. A curved decoration is carved into its surface. Its base continues beneath two other monuments.

scholar_tomb.title: The Crystal Monument
scholar_tomb.description:
The black-and-white crystal catches a faint light. Beneath a carved creature, a thin fragment is sealed inside. Something seems to be drawn on it.
Around forty-five years ago, the fragment may still have been clear enough to make out the drawing. Compare the foot of the monument as it is now with how it looked about forty-five years ago. Look for any trace of a later visit.

sun_tomb.title: The Sun-Shaped Monument
sun_tomb.description:
Radiating points surround a small creature whose two halves look entirely different. The stone base beneath it extends to join two other markers.
The wishing pool nearby may still have held an offering around sixty years ago when it's still in use. It might be worth looking into the basin. Someone may have left something here when the civilization was still alive and the conflict was just starting.

altar_tomb.title: The White Infant Altar
altar_tomb.description:
A grand house-shaped memorial in the cramped underground cemetery. An infant rests on its white platform. An unending path runs along the pillars, the recess below is nearly empty, and one symbol is still unreadable.
Try looking at the recess and platform as they were fifty years ago.

mother_tomb.title: The Small Stone Beside the Altar
mother_tomb.description:
An unassuming stone stands beside the great altar. Geometric pictures cover its face: a figure with a child above, two figures reaching toward each other below, and cracked lines around the edge.
Compare the ground beside the stone today with the same spot about forty-five years ago. Did anyone return to leave something there? A stain on the face of the stone might have been brighter when she's alive.

father_tomb.title: The Other Stone Beside the Altar
father_tomb.description:
Another modest stone stands on the other side of the altar. A figure carries a child above a crystal-like figure. Along the border, a smaller figure climbs an upward path.
About fifty years ago, someone may have left a small offering beside the stone.

girl_tomb.title: The Solitary Human-Shaped Marker
girl_tomb.description:
Another human figure stands within a frame of pale stone. She seems older than the child on the small marker. A two-part creature and an unending path decorate the frame. The stone is embedded too deeply to measure its thickness.
The paint on the stone may also have been easier to see then.

designer_manuscript.title: A Marker for Someone Without an Occupation
designer_manuscript.body:
A translated copy of designer manuscript
Our cemetery usually represents a person through an icon of their occupation. This burial is different: the deceased is an infant who had not yet been assigned an occupation. None of the existing designs would do.

The family asked us not to define the child by work he had never begun. We chose a human figure instead. The child had no occupation, but he was still a person.

"A child without an occupation is a person before anything else."

designer_journal.title: A Page of the Designer's Journal
designer_journal.body: My student visited me with urgency. She showed me a photo of the actual appearance of the infant. I was stunned as I never saw a dayfolk that was born like this. She asked me to design the tombstone with his real appearance, so that he can truly be remembered. I rejected her, as I have having a commission from the infant's parents, not her. She left with disappointment, and perhaps, a little bit of anger.

Authorization: Both parents signed the consent form.

disappearance_inquiry.title: The Scholar's Notes on Disappearances
disappearance_inquiry.body:
The unexplained disappearances in Day City are always reported at dawn, when people wake.

The Dayfolk's bodies are unusual. Anyone who fails to enter a sleeping coffin on time will die. Once inside, however, they lose all awareness and ability to act for the entire night, under the coffin's complete protection.

Who has been tampering with their sleeping coffins? I cannot investigate the movements of the Nightfolks while they are awake. I can only suspect that, while taking our food, they have also done something to my husband and my people.

It is not only disappearances. Many of us, myself included, have found fresh wounds upon waking. Given the Nightfolk's habit of plundering, they are most likely responsible. I must remain vigilant.

profession_record.title: The Scholar, Her Work, and Her Patron
profession_record.body:
The record describes a Day City resident who first studied this transparent mineral and discovered the energy within it. She was granted the title of Scholar.

The stones were later used to power machinery. The occupational title thus became associated with crystal research.

A young man from a wealthy family was the first to invest in her research. He later became her husband and came to be known as the Tycoon.

In recognition of her outstanding contributions to Day City, the Scholar may apply for a mausoleum beyond the usual grave-marker design and have her family interred within it. For the Dayfolk, who place such importance on the rituals of death, this is the highest honor.

one_way_passage_order.title: An Order for a One-Way Passage
one_way_passage_order.body:
An order to the Scholar: We must put an end to Nightfolk incursions at their source.

They were once allowed to take our food in exchange for the crystals they excavated. Now they neglect their work, yet continue to demand more and more from Day City.

A one-way passage must be established: the Dayfolk may descend, but the Nightfolk must not be allowed to ascend.

twin_beast_account.title: An Account of the Twin-Bodied Creature
twin_beast_account.body:
Legend tells of a twin-bodied creature that lived here before Day City was founded. Its two halves looked entirely different: one was covered in fur, with narrow eyes; the other was smooth, with clearly visible eyes.

Then, in a single night, they disappeared.

The oldest account places the creature here 250 years ago. If it ever walked these grounds, a trace of it might still be found under the searchlight.

skyway_history.title: An Account of the Skyway
skyway_history.body:
The Skyway is a path cleared upward through fallen stone. It is uneven, but not steep.

Searching for food and water, the Nightfolk dug and climbed in every direction. At last, they opened a route upward through the collapsed ruins.

The Dayfolk called the day they arrived "the Day Darkness Descended." Much food and many livestock were taken before the Dayfolk even knew who had done it. Eventually, they discovered the passage to Night City.

The reopened route also led the Dayfolk to the shining stones the Nightfolk had excavated while searching for food and water: crystals that would later power Day City's development.

The exchange continued with each cycle of day and night. The Dayfolk brought back crystals; the Nightfolk brought back food. Each took what they needed. This balance lasted a long time.
skyway_history.interactive_body:
The Skyway is a path cleared upward through fallen stone. It is uneven, but not steep.

Searching for food and water, the Nightfolk dug and climbed in every direction. At last, they opened a route upward through the collapsed ruins.

The Dayfolk called the day they arrived "the Day Darkness Descended." Much food and many livestock were taken before the Dayfolk even knew who had done it. Eventually, they discovered the passage to Night City.

The reopened route also led the Dayfolk to the shining stones the Nightfolk had excavated while searching for food and water: crystals that would later power Day City's development.

The exchange continued with each cycle of day and night. The Dayfolk brought back crystals; the Nightfolk brought back food. Each took what they needed. This balance lasted a long time.

title: An Account of the Skyway

day_city_history.title: A History of Day City
day_city_history.body:
This history was a banned book until it was discovered.

Both Dayfolk and Nightfolk must rest in their sleeping coffins at the proper time if they are to awaken the following day.

Before their division, they were known together as the People of Sun and Moon. Some had the daylight; others had the moonlit night.

In their shared residential districts, sleeping coffins stood upright to conserve space. Later, when the Nightfolk moved underground, the number of people on the surface decreased. Space was no longer scarce, and the Dayfolk developed the habit of lying down in their coffins.

The Nightfolk placed theirs underground, where the darkness of the caves made them almost indistinguishable from the surrounding floor.

girl_diary.title: A Diary Page, Author Unknown
girl_diary.body:
If the truth of death itself is being covered up, then am I not an accomplice when I carve monuments to that lie?

I can no longer bear this hypocritical world. If even one person had stopped to question what was wrong with the world we lived in, perhaps we would never have come to this.

I once loved and respected my mother so much. She was my example from childhood. But first she failed to protect my brother; then she blamed my father's disappearance on others. Even when I tried to tell her the truth about our world, she insisted that useless sympathy would destroy Day City.

How many more times must we hurt our own people in the name of protecting them?

She left me a message on my windowsill when she came to the Day City. She is so intelligent that she acquired the language of Day City just by observing the surroundings and reading the library, and she found out my identity as her correspondence just by the messages conveyed by the stones. She said there was an old site in the ruins, with sleeping coffins that could keep the two of us alive.

She told me why she wanted to leave. Before her brother was born, she had a place in the family. Afterwards, every hope and every tenderness seemed to belong to him. When he disappeared, she waited for her parents to notice that she was still there. Instead, their grief filled the place he had left. Night City called them the Holy Father and Holy Mother. She could not remember the last time she had felt like their daughter.

I wanted to leave a world my mother kept defending. She wanted to leave a home where she felt unseen. Neither of us would bring our mother. With my mother's influence in Day City, everyone would find out if she came. For the other girl, leaving without hers was the point.

I have to persuade her. We can only escape on our own. The One-way Passage Order is launching soon. We need to act fast.

lines.speaker: #PLAYER#
lines.content: Oh, my notebook’s in black and white.

lines.speaker: #PLAYER#
lines.content: Aurora never told me why. I guess it’s an aesthetic choice.
...Hello? Can you hear me?
(It doesn't take you a second to realize who's speaking. That's the first time you hear her voice beyond your textual exchange. Her voice is huskier than you thought.)

lines.speaker: #PLAYER#
lines.content: Aurora? Is that you? The connection’s finally back. I’ve landed safely on Twins.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Glad you’re safe! I hope the trip wasn’t too rough. Have you had a chance to look through your handbook?

lines.speaker: #PLAYER#
lines.content: Yeah, I was just looking at it. Interesting color scheme.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: There’s a reason for it. Seen from space, Twins is a planet in black and white... Just like the civilization that once lived there. Of course, that’s a bonus to the name. It was first named the Twins because its day and night align with Earth’s, despite the distance between them.

lines.speaker: #PLAYER#
lines.content: Should I expect to meet anyone here?

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: No, but you’ll find their traces—a fallen civilization of two cities. Our archaeologists have searched their libraries, their homes, their schools. All the places where they lived. But there’s one place they overlooked.

lines.speaker: #PLAYER#
lines.content: Where?
(You might have an answer in mind. But you wait for her confirmation.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Where they remembered the dead. The cemeteries. That’s your mission: to uncover what words alone cannot tell us, through the memories they left behind.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: We don’t have much transmission time left. I have to go. Talk to you later.
(Now it’s just you, your handbook, and the faint breath of the planet.)
(You feel a tremor in your limbs.)
(You stand up. The faint breeze brushing past your ears feels much like the wind back home. Perhaps the people who once lived here weren’t so different from you, either.)
(You’re here to gather their memories. Your steps grow steadier.)
(Then you see it: the place where an entire civilization rests.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: You didn't expect a call from her. But she'd like to talk to you briefly. She wants this call to be brief, so you can only ask the two questions you’re most curious about.
(She pauses once, then sets the explanation down plainly.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: They have separate minds and take turns being awake. They share one living body. If one dies, the other cannot survive. The Dayfolk acted as if they could cut that dependence away.
(A small silence falls across the name. She answers without decorating it.)
(A small silence falls across the name. She answers without decorating it.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Aurora is a name. It does not tell you how many people are speaking, or how many points of view they have. It's never in your record.
(You hear a dry, almost amused breath. She chooses an example close to your own life.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Think of two people taking turns using one account. The account is closed. Neither can enter, but only one receives the notice. The other has no record of what happened. That is how something can die for one person and disappear for the other.
(Her answer begins firmly. A quieter note enters when she mentions the shared cemetery.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: No. There was a cemetery where both peoples were buried together. You will not visit it on this trip. They did not always keep their graves separate, nor their residences. If you learn about cemeteries in human civilization, they are often the microcosm of a city's history of integration and segregation—cemeteries are the diorama of cities.
(She lets out a quiet breath and brings the discussion back to the task.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I have to drop. See ya.
(The wind echoes through the city no one has returned to. It might be your imagination, but it feels colder now.)
(You can't tell. We keep losing memories at every moment. Words said in the last moment, a warm smile that you pass by a minute ago, and those fleeting and private feelings attached to them.)
“We feel, and all that we have felt is swept away in the bright tumult of the world.”
(You first read Goethe's poem An Lottchen from Zweig's The World of Yesterday, where he recounts the beautiful world before the war that strips us of our humanity.)
(It is only when you witness a collapse that you realize how fragile our established routines can be. You wonder whether…)
(You are not sure if the Day Aurora will call back when the night ends. But you look to the horizon, and see a beautiful light shine from the back of the solitary stone.)
(No matter what—on Earth or these obsolete cities. Tomorrow the sun will rise.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Yes, it does look like a moon. I suppose sleep is the closest rehearsal the living have for death. When night falls, the Dayfolk slip into slumber. On this marker, the moon stands for natural death.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The outline is a starting point. Show me your comparison with the moon, and we can ask what it meant to the Dayfolk.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The moon offers a peaceful ending, but that is the story the family chose to put in stone. If the child's real face was left out, perhaps there were unexplained circumstances behind his death. Let us keep looking.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Before we ask why, perhaps we should ask why not. Day City remembers a life through its work. This child was the first to die without an identifiable occupation. So the designer gave him something no title was needed for: the shape of a person.

("A child without an occupation is a person before anything else,” you were reminded of the quote from the manuscript. Despite the punchline, or slogan that speaks to everyone else but the infant, can he really separate from the social influence?)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Yes, this is an icon for the Dayfolk. Have you found a designer's manuscript that explains why this marker was shaped like a person?

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Compare the rubbing with the figure in the cemetery. What do the two shapes have in common?

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I cannot tell you who drew it, #PLAYER#. Perhaps someone had grown tired of seeing the same approved face carved over every life that did not fit.
(She seems to have personal feelings about this topic.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: As the manuscript says, they gave her the title Scholar when she discovered what the crystal could do. Her stone remembers that work in the very material she studied—the work she was truly proud of.

(You can't help thinking back to the moment when you first saw the crystal in the Night City. Unlike its transparency in the Day City, the enigmatic darkness draws you in and makes you wonder how these beautiful stones changed Day and Night.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The crystal had a history before it became a memorial. #PLAYER#, find its mineral counterpart, or the record of the work it made possible.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: On one stone, a creature might have belonged to a single life. When it keeps turning up on graves that have nothing else in common, I start to wonder what the whole city needed a way to say.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Look for a pattern like that in Night City. If the same sign turns up on several graves there, ask yourself what those people kept leaving for one another. They may have had something quite different to say.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The old account says the creature vanished in a single night. These little figures seem to carry that absence from stone to stone. They record disappearance. You may find other traces of what disappearance meant for the Dayfolk.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: A familiar shape can travel from grave to grave without telling us its name. Look for the creature beyond these stones, #PLAYER#. Perhaps a trace of it—or the same icon returning again and again.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: This is an important step. Food went down; crystal came up. For a long while, each city worked to produce something the other needed. The stone has kept a little of that old dependence — though there is still insufficient evidence to establish whether they shared any aspect of life.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I would be careful about asking a single stone to speak for two cities. We need some evidence that passed between them.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The gate was meant to close behind anyone going down. Its crystal power supply ran for far longer than it was designed to. The mechanism failed years ago, with the gate open. That’s how you’ve been able to cross in both directions.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I cannot speak for her. But I believe she must have discovered something about the world she lived in. Some truth she could not leave out of her own memorial. Your notebook is black and white for a reason, too.
(You look at your notebook once again. One double-page spread accommodating two contrasting halves. Does it signal a kind of coexistence, or a history of segregation?)
(The name of neither city comes easily. A tiny catch in her breathing survives the distance intact.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: A Dayfolk and a Nightfolk, hand in hand... I never expected her to be so cruel to herself.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I cannot make out the picture, but I am fairly sure that fragment is skin — from past research, we know that the Dayfolk have blue blood, and some of it remains on the fragment. Try the searchlight. Take it back to a time before it decayed, before we decide what it was trying to say.

(For a long while, only the thin electrical hum reaches you. Then a breath catches, and leaves her in a long, uneven sigh. You cannot see her, but for once the distance fails to conceal how much the question has touched her.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: …or there is no one left to remember her. I made that decision. I made that decision...

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: You are perceptive. Dayfolk and Nightfolk share one life. A wound left on one body is still there when the other wakes. Few people discovered they could send a message that way. Most called the injuries Nightfolk retaliation. The misunderstanding only widened the divide between the cities.
(A small intake of breath. When she answers, the warmth has returned a little too neatly, like a blanket pulled over something that is still moving.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I imagine anyone would be moved, #PLAYER#. To make your own skin carry a message—well. We need not have known her to feel that. Shall we return to the investigation?

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: So many stones have borrowed the same creature. Its vanishing in the old account gives the carving its meaning: disappearance. An image left behind where a life cannot be found.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The creature keeps returning, doesn't it? Let us give it a name before we give it a meaning. What does the old account say?
(Perhaps use your tools to observe those markers again.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Yes. One unbroken base carries all three. They belong to the same family plot. The stone has kept them together, even after their stories parted.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Look beneath their feet. A family resemblance may be written in the stone they stand on. Are their bases truly joined?

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: ...I have nothing to tell.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: She left it.
(The answer comes before the question has quite left the channel. Then there is a silence just long enough for you to hear what slipped through.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I have to go. Goodbye.
(Silence. Only the buzzing sound reminds you that the call is not interrupted.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Someone was still there after the others were gone. I wonder whether the family left a place for her, or whether she had already begun to leave it herself.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: It is the Crystal God, the Nightfolk's sign of faith. Left on a grave, it is also a blessing: “To disappear is to set out on a journey without end. May the wishes of crystal remain with you.” It wishes the departed well.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Photograph the same sign on all three graves first. Bring me that record, and I can read it for you.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Day City records a death. Night City records a disappearance. That difference does not mean there were two children. Check the figures together.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Compare the figures first, then we'll see.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Not everything can be interpreted with a modern mindset, and not all offerings are intended for commercial exchange. These are blessings given by the Nightfolk.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Show me the stones first.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The Crystal God stood there intact. The crystals were later pried out. Day City needed crystal, but I cannot prove they did it. For now, you can take this as a provisional argument.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Use the searchlight on the empty recess. We need to see what was there.
(You look from the carving to the crystal in the scene. The outline is the same, and for a moment the sign seems less carved than set down.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Set the stone beside the carving: the same facets, the same point at the top. The Nightfolk did not picture their god as a person. They carved the crystal itself.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: It is what they dug from the dark and came to trust. A figure made of that stone is faith, and it is also a blessing: “May the wishes of crystal remain with you.”
(The silence lasts just a fraction longer than the question seems to need. Her reply is direct.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: A symbol can be remembered without a written language. Someone who used it could pass on its meaning. I am not working from books alone.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Check the division first. If it was wrong, 'born in the wrong city' may be the wrong question. Keep the two memorials together.
(Her voice stops abruptly. The night spills around you, with barely a sound. You start to think about how the Day City looked, and your call with Aurora then.)
(It's different, definitely. Two worlds overlap in the dimension of time.)
(Was it "wrong"? Or is it just a glimpse through the overlap?)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: That is the altar infant. The figure is his mother in Night City.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Compare the child with the altar infant. That will tell us who she was holding.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The border matches the dry riverbed. It records hunger and thirst as her cause of death.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The symbol means a dry river. Check the actual riverbed or the records of lost water before we conclude that she died of hunger and thirst.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The wounds carried over when the other person woke. A mark on the shared body could carry a message between them.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The pictures match. But the medium is unknown.
(The hiss of the open line grows suddenly loud. Her answer returns without its usual firmness.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: No sign of anyone returning. She may have been the last. I used to think she would only notice me if I went missing too. I left. I never found out whether she did.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: One empty scan is not enough. Check the period after her burial.
(She is quiet long enough for the static to return. When she speaks, she leaves no space between the short sentences.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: A flower. A mother and daughter drew it for each other when the girl was small. It meant "I love you." Just between them.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: It is not a blessing used throughout Night City. This one belonged to those two people.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Show me the flower the searchlight recovered. We should not assume that every painted mark is a funerary symbol.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The same child. Look at the way he is held. The man carrying him is his father in Night City.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Match the child with the altar figure before you name the parent.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The path was uneven, but it was not a dangerous climb. He kept searching beyond the permitted waking hours and failed to reach a sleeping coffin in time.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Check the actual path or its history. An upward line does not show how steep it was.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: One dies. The other disappears at dawn. Check whether these are two records of one life.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Bring the Scholar's disappearance report. We need the time her husband vanished.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: It is a blessing for the person who left. Nobody was paying for the path.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Record the stone. Compare it with the altar offerings.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The history calls it natural. Shared coffins weaken the claim that there was no room. They do not prove who caused the collapse. We need separate evidence for that.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: An upright sleeping coffin, just like the old illustration. A change in how people slept can leave a surprisingly long shadow.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: That frame has an older history than the girl inside it. Let us look for its shape in the book.
(For a moment, the sentence seems to cost her more than it should.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The diary writer carved memorials and came to question the stories they were asked to preserve. She was a funerary artist. Perhaps this was the one stone she could finally let speak for herself.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: A human shape can stand for many lives. Her work may have left a clearer signature in the diary.
(She draws out the first word, then presses the rest into an even rhythm. You hear how much work the evenness takes.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The diary gives the two girls different reasons to leave. One could no longer bear what her mother defended. The other had spent years waiting to be noticed, first beside her brother, then beside the space he left. Their departure was deliberate. A memorial can mark an absence without proving a death.
(The silence feels less like thought than resistance. You wait until it gives way.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Read what she meant to do. A stone can remember an absence without knowing where the person went.
You are about to ask Aurora about the girl on the cover. Are you ready to begin the final conversation?

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I didn't know she had the privilege of doing so, yet she never did. She was someone who valued reputation and recognition; she lived her life in the prescribed mold of a successful Dayfolk. But she never mentioned the mausoleum again. Why?
(The next line is so faint that it sounds like a whisper to herself.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: She might be feeling as guilty as…
(The last few words disperse in the humming sound.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I'm not sure whether the Scholar is eligible… Have you found any evidence related to that?

lines.speaker: #PLAYER#
lines.content: You seem to know the link between disappearance and death, which proves the Scholar's speculation wrong. You know much more than I do. I want to know:

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: You saw that conflict — the Scholar ended up using skin as a medium to convey a message, proving her initial conclusion that the scars were caused by the Nightfolk wrong. This does not directly prove her conclusion about disappearance wrong, but I would encourage you to investigate along this thread.
(You can feel the strong implication behind her words. It feels like she knows everything but is still toying with you. You wonder if she will tell you where she's from and what she has done.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The Dayfolk often get stuck in their own understanding of the world. You may want to find more conflicts between the world they firmly believe in and the actual world around us.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: They have separate minds and take turns being awake. They share one living body. If one dies, the other cannot survive. What one city records as death, the other may record as disappearance.
(Her voice fractures, just like the world you are standing in, a world that belongs to yesterday.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I am someone who belongs to this place, yet something stops me from going back.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: A path that does not end and does not return.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I have heard that idea before, in one of the translations I gave you: a journey without end. Look back through my words, and bring me the one that says it.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: That is it. “A journey without end”: the blessing and this path say the same thing. Someone left and did not return, and the Nightfolk call that disappearance.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: It does not tell us what happened to that person.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: It represents a river that has run dry. That is the meaning of the symbol. Whether it describes this place, a loss of water, or the circumstances of her death needs further evidence.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: A path leading upward, toward the surface. It records a journey. It does not tell us how steep the path was or why the traveller died.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The Crystal God. It marks faith in the deity, and the Nightfolk also leave it on graves as a blessing for the departed. The same figure can appear on an altar or a personal memorial; its presence alone does not tell us who removed the crystals.
(You almost asked that question, but deep down, you know why it’s here.)
(You decided not to ask this way.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Anything else?

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I'm not sure what you are talking about.
(If your guess is correct, she might not know. You decided to keep this question for later.)

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: Anything else?

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: I'm confused.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The Crystal God, left as a shared blessing. It appears on graves of different people because it belongs to a custom, not to one person.

lines.speaker: Aurora
lines.content: The Nightfolk wish the departed well. The same sign, left again and again, makes that wish something the whole city can recognise.
